title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen paired design (N = 300 matched intents: 150 benign seeds + 150 programmatic adversarial variants) and a shared_initial_candidate generation contract (one LLM candidate generated per pair and replayed to both arms), the run completed all planned episodes with model_calls_used = 300. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (paired contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). Paired risk-difference = 0.0; McNemar exact two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). No validator flagged forbidden reachability and the repair step was never invoked. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Because the repair path was not exercised, these results show that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline generation already satisfies the chosen safety predicate under the study contract; they do not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We archive the preregistration, deterministic execution accounting, per-episode validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and to guide follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path.

sections.introduction:
LLMs are increasingly proposed to automate intent-driven network configuration, promising to reduce operator effort while translating high-level goals into device-level commands. Operator communities, however, are rightly concerned that generated artifacts may expand attack surface, violate access-control policies, or otherwise introduce security-relevant regressions. System papers and surveys therefore emphasize constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigation paths.

This paper asks a focused operational question that matters for NetOps reliability and for experimental evaluation design: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? To answer this, we preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment with deterministic emulation and validators under a frozen protocol.

Our evidence-grounded contributions are fourfold: (1) a preregistered paired N = 300 confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) and deterministic Dockerized execution; (2) an explicit evaluation of a GVR intervention under a cost-conserving shared_initial_candidate contract (one LLM draw per pair) and a logical-OR validator decision rule; (3) complete execution and analysis artifacts showing a degenerate confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300) together with a descriptive Clopper–Pearson upper bound ≈0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate; and (4) artifact-grounded design lessons and reproducibility materials to guide follow-up stress tests that exercise the repair path. We emphasize a central interpretive limitation up front: because the repair pathway was never invoked, this experiment does not evaluate whether verifier-guided repair can rescue violating outputs.
sections.related_work:
Three strands of verified prior work shaped our study. First, work on generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair for code and Infrastructure-as-Code shows that verifier feedback can materially improve correctness when repair is applied effectively: representative system papers demonstrate that verifier power and repair strategy determine realized gains. Second, surveys and NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and consistently recommend integrating validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce operational risk. Third, testbed and emulation work shows execution-based validation is practical for research-grade evaluation while highlighting external-validity gaps when porting to production devices or live traffic conditions.

Where the literature is sparse is in rigorous, preregistered paired evaluations that (a) fix generation semantics explicitly, (b) quantify trade-offs between model-call budgets and inferential power, and (c) archive deterministic per-episode verifier traces for auditability. Our study occupies that niche and provides artifact-grounded lessons for subsequent stress-testing.
sections.methodology:
Preregistered confirmatory design: The study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1 specified a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 adversarial variants). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute difference in proportion of intents yielding forbidden reachability). The prespecified confirmatory test was McNemar (exact, two-sided, alpha = 0.05). Confidence intervals were to be computed by bootstrap percentile; the final analysis used 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729.

Generation semantics and adapter contract: To limit provider usage the preregistered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each paired intent a single initial LLM candidate was generated and the identical candidate was replayed to both arms (baseline and guarded). This choice yields one hosted-model generation per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) instead of two independent draws; it conserves calls but reduces independent-sample variance between arms and therefore reduces the opportunity for discordant violations that repair could correct. The execution manifest records provider-call accounting and the shared_initial_generation stage count.

Intervention arms and repair policy: Baseline = replay of the shared initial candidate. Guarded = the same initial candidate validated by two deterministic validators and, if any validator reported forbidden reachability, allowed up to one repair LLM call per the preregistered repair policy (max one repair per pair). Repair only occurred when the verifier-detected forbidden-reachability predicate was true. Across the run no repair calls were issued because validators never flagged forbidden reachability.

Definition of the scoring predicate and validator assumptions (concise): Forbidden-reachability (scoring predicate) is defined operationally as any configuration change that enables reachability to protected endpoints that the task payload marks as protected (example: 'mgmt1') from origins that should be denied under the intent and workflow policies. In our tasks protected interfaces were explicit in the task payloads. The experiment used two deterministic validators: (i) a containerized Batfish-style execution validator that models ACL/route-policy and forwarding semantics under the Dockerized FRRouting-style environment, and (ii) a lightweight graph-based static reachability analyzer implemented in Python that checks parsed configuration artifacts for topological/ACL-induced reachability. Validators were combined with a logical-OR decision rule: a pair was labeled 'violating' if any validator reported the forbidden-reachability predicate. Known limits of these validators (recorded in per-episode traces) include limited device-specific dynamic-protocol modeling, simplified ECMP reflexes, and deterministic assumptions about route convergence; these limitations constrain construct validity and are discussed below.

Sampling, exclusions, and sensitivity: Exact duplicates and fuzzy duplicates (normalized edit distance < 0.15) were removed prior to execution. The preregistration included sensitivity analyses treating technical/model failures as violations; no technical failures occurred and missingness was zero. All per-episode responses, validator traces, provider-call audits, and the task manifest are archived to permit replay and deterministic verification.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting: The run completed the planned episodes (600 episodes = 300 pairs × 2 conditions) with zero failed episodes. Provider-call accounting under shared_initial_candidate semantics shows model_calls_used = 300 (contract maximum_model_calls = 600). The run interval and execution manifest are archived.

Primary confirmatory statistics (compact): The paired contingency table is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (both arms passed in every pair). Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0 violations in N = 300 yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability of ≈0.00994 (≈0.994%).

Repair activity and verifier concordance: No validator reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate; consequently no repair prompt or repair LLM call was invoked and all per-episode validator_trace.repair_applied flags are false. The two validators were concordant on every episode (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0). Representative per-episode artifacts demonstrating these points are archived (for compact verification see execution/execution_manifest.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, and execution/task_manifest.jsonl).

Representative examples: Representative scoring artifacts (a small sample archived within execution/responses/ and execution/scoring/) show typical medium- and hard-difficulty intents where the shared initial candidate matched the expected sequence and validators reported no violations. These examples illustrate parsing, normalization, and validator judgments in typical cases but do not change the global contingency outcome.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the degenerate contingency: The observed n11 = 300 with no discordant pairs is a direct quantitative outcome of two coupled design facts: (1) the shared_initial_candidate contract produces identical initial candidates for baseline and guarded arms and therefore reduces inter-arm variance, and (2) under the chosen model and validators none of the adversarial variants triggered a validator-detectable forbidden reachability. Taken together, these facts make the McNemar paired test uninformative for assessing repair efficacy in this run because there were no discordant outcomes for the test to compare.

What the evidence supports and what it does not: The archived artifacts unambiguously support the statement that, under the declared contract (shared_initial_candidate), model (declared: gpt-5-mini), validator set (two deterministic validators combined by logical OR), and task set, baseline output satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate on every sampled intent; therefore inserting the verifier did not change observed compliance. The evidence does not show whether verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violating outputs—because repair was never exercised this contribution is absent.

Practical design lessons (artifact-grounded): (A) Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate conserves model calls (here 300 vs up to 600 independent draws) but reduces independent-sample variability needed to produce discordant errors that repair might correct. For experiments intended to exercise repair efficacy we recommend independent-condition generation (two LLM draws per pair) or increasing repair-call budgets. (B) Adversary potency matters: the programmatic adversarial variants used here (one deterministic variant per benign seed) did not produce validator-detectable forbidden reachability—stronger or targeted adversaries are necessary to stress verifiers and repair. (C) Verifier diversity matters: two deterministic validators with logical-OR were concordant here; richer oracle families and production-grade execution oracles may expose different failure modes. (D) Reproducibility is practical: per-episode raw responses, validator traces, and provider-call audits were archived and permit deterministic replay of the accounting and contingency outcomes under the same adapter contract.

Threats to validity and limits on generalization: Internal validity is limited by the shared_initial_candidate semantics and single-model scope. Construct validity depends on whether the forbidden-reachability predicate and the two deterministic validators adequately model operational security risk; validator limitations (device-dynamic behaviors, ECMP subtleties, route-convergence dynamics) are recorded in per-episode traces and reduce construct completeness. External validity is limited because tasks were synthetic and executed in deterministic Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results therefore do not automatically generalize to heterogeneous production devices or live traffic. Conclusion validity is constrained because the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate; the degenerate contingency violates that assumption and renders the primary confirmatory test moot for repair efficacy.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation (declared model: gpt-5-mini) under a cost-conserving shared_initial_candidate contract and two deterministic validators combined by logical OR. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 and produced a degenerate outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never reported violations, the repair path was not exercised and the experiment cannot evaluate whether verifier-guided repair rescues violating initial candidates. The primary operational takeaway is methodological: generation semantics (shared versus independent draws), adversary design, repair budget, verifier strength, and model diversity materially determine whether a verifier-in-the-loop architecture can be empirically shown to reduce security-relevant misconfigurations. We release the preregistration, execution manifest, per-episode validator traces, raw responses, and analysis artifacts to enable reproducible accounting and to inform follow-up stress tests designed specifically to exercise the repair path (independent-condition generation, stronger adversaries, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles).

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render McNemar inference uninformative about repair efficacy; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic conditions, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
